query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding titanium to the BCC NbMoTaW alloy will improve its room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance while preserving its high-temperature mechanical performance and BCC structural stability.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution due to titanium addition
generation.predicted_outcome: 20% increase in room-temperature ductility and 15% increase in irradiation tolerance compared to untreated NbMoTaW
generation.boundary: Temperature: up to 1600 °C, Irradiation: helium implantation
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of titanium to be added and the potential effects on the alloy's microstructure and phase stability are uncertain

falsification_experiment.design: Tensile testing and helium implantation experiments
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy's room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance do not increase by at least 10% compared to untreated NbMoTaW, the hypothesis is falsified

He defined high-entropy alloys (HEAs) as having five or more major elements beneath 5–35 at.%, and minor elements below five at.%. In 2006, he also established four core effects of HEAs []: High-entropy, severe-lattices-distortion, sluggish-diffusion, and the cocktail effect. With the new concepts, scientists are able to develop and expand alloys without restrictions [,,,,]. Some HEAs have been found to have attractive properties on diffusion [], oxidation [], corrosion [], fatigue [], creep [], fracture toughness [], and elevated-temperature strength []. High-entropy superalloys (HESAs) [], eutectic HEAs (EHEAs) [], light-weight HEAs (LWHEAs) [], refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) [], etc. have been proposed and attract increased attention. AbstractMedium-entropy alloys (MEAs) are prospective structural materials for emerging advanced nuclear systems because of their outstanding mechanical properties and irradiation resistance. In this study, the microstructure and mechanical properties of three new single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) structured MEAs (Zr40Nb35Ti25, Zr50Nb35Ti15, and Zr60Nb35Ti5) before and after irradiation were investigated. It is shown that the yield strength and elongation after fracture at room temperature are greater than 900 MPa and 10%, respectively. Three MEAs were irradiated with 3 MeV Fe11+ ions to 8 × 1015 and 2.5 × 1016 ions/cm2 at temperatures of 300 and 500 °C, to investigate the irradiation-induced hardening and microstructure changes. Compared with most conventional alloys, the three MEAs showed only negligible irradiation hardening and even softening in some cases. After irradiation, they exhibit somewhat surprising lattice constant reduction, and the microstructure contains small dislocation loops. Neither cavities nor precipitates were observed.
